rejected.title: Māori responses to colonisation
card: Māori are the Indigenous people of Aotearoa New Zealand. Māori responded to the arrival of the British in different ways, and not all Māori responded in the same way.
Trade
Many Māori traded with the British. They sold goods such as food and flax, and gained tools and other goods in return.
Negotiation
In 1840 many Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi with the British Crown. The English and Māori versions of the Treaty differed, and this led to disputes.
Resistance
Later, as settlers wanted more land, Māori fought to defend their land. These conflicts are called the New Zealand Wars.
rejected.remember: Māori traded with, negotiated with and resisted the British, and land was at the centre of the conflict.

a.q: Which event is an example of Māori negotiating with the British?
opts: Many chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840
Māori fought battles over land in the New Zealand Wars
Māori sold food and flax to British visitors
Māori left their land to settle in Australia
a.why: Signing the Treaty was an agreement made by talking with the British Crown, so it is negotiation. Selling food and flax is trade, and the wars were resistance by fighting.
a.clue: Negotiation means reaching an agreement through discussion.

b.q: In the 1860s, settlers in Taranaki wanted more land, and some Māori groups took up arms to keep their land. Which response does this show?
opts: Resistance, as part of the New Zealand Wars
Trade, as part of an exchange of goods
Negotiation, as part of signing the Treaty
Acceptance, as the British had a right to the land
b.why: Taking up arms to defend land is resistance, and these conflicts are called the New Zealand Wars. The Treaty was signed in 1840 and was a negotiation, so it is not the best answer here even though the conflict was linked to land.
b.clue: Look at what the Māori groups did to keep their land.

version.title: Māori responses to colonisation
card: Māori, the Indigenous people of Aotearoa New Zealand, did not respond to the British as one group. Responses changed over time and differed between iwi (tribes).
Trade
from the early 1800s, many Māori traded with Europeans, exchanging flax, timber and food for tools, muskets and other goods.
Negotiation
in 1840 more than 500 Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi with the British Crown. Its English and Māori texts differed in meaning, which led to lasting disputes.
Resistance
as settlers pressed for more land, some Māori groups fought British and colonial forces in the New Zealand Wars, mainly from the 1840s to the 1870s.
version.remember: Māori met the British with trade, treaty talks and war, and land was at the heart of the fighting.

a.q: Why did the Treaty of Waitangi lead to disputes after it was signed?
opts: Its English and Māori texts did not mean the same
No Māori chiefs agreed to sign it in 1840
It was signed by traders, not by the Crown
It banned all trade between Māori and settlers
a.why: The English and Māori texts of the Treaty differed in meaning, so each side could understand the agreement differently. It was signed by more than 500 chiefs and the British Crown, not by traders.
a.clue: Think about the two languages it was written in.

b.q: In the 1860s, settlers in the Waikato wanted Māori land, and Māori groups fought colonial troops to keep it. Which response does this show?
opts: Resistance, in the New Zealand Wars
Negotiation, in the Treaty of Waitangi
Trade, in an exchange of flax for tools
Resistance, in the signing of the Treaty
b.why: Fighting to keep land is resistance, and the conflicts of this time are called the New Zealand Wars. The Treaty was signed in 1840 through negotiation, so the fighting was not part of it.
b.clue: Look at what the Māori groups did, and when.
